title: Seven Deadly Fitness Sins: Wrath
summary: Second entry in his seven-deadly-sins series, on wrath. He argues that lifting angry gives a real short-term boost but is unsustainable, pushes people to seek out bad experiences to refuel it, and bleeds aggression into home life. He now trains in a cold, calculated way with short bursts of intensity and insists the gym should drain negative energy so you come home calm.

claims.claim: A lot of people in the YouTube fitness community are extremely angry, at themselves or at others, often feeling lied to or inadequate compared to others.
Being mean online means nothing for the target; it mostly reveals the insecurity of the person writing it.
Lifting angry gives an aggressive energy boost, and some of his best sets ever came from shouting through a heavy set fueled by anger.
Anger as training fuel is not sustainable: lifting tires you out and the anger eventually runs dry, leaving you with a mindset that only knows how to make gains through rage.
People who rely on anger to lift tend to get stuck recreating bad experiences to keep the anger fueled, which damages both their lifting and their life.
Using the gym to unload the day's stress is fine, but you must leave the aggression there and re-enter family life calm; bringing the beast home is unfair to the people around you.
Wrath becomes a capital sin when you let it take over your life and become your personality.

During a period when he channeled anger at people into lifting, he became aggressive with people outside the gym and caught himself calling up bad memories to fuel heavy lifts, which is when he decided to stop.
His current approach is cold and calculated, using only very short bursts of energy and motivation when needed; breaking the anger cycle made his life outside the gym much better.
Lifting matters a lot to him but it is not his number one priority; his family is.

The gym should be a place to deplete negative energy so you can be chill at home; from years in competitive sports he saw many athletes fail to switch off and carry that intensity into daily life, where it hurts more than it helps.
Reflecting on the seven capital sins is an intellectual exercise for him to spot behaviours he still needs to work on to become a better person.
